article.title: When Random Sampling Is Not Enough: Why Experiments Use Stratification
article.why: Practical analytical English for data-driven decisions.

paragraphs.en: Random assignment is the foundation of a controlled experiment because, in expectation, it balances observed and unobserved characteristics between treatment and control groups. Yet randomization does not guarantee perfect balance in one realized sample. When an outcome is rare, important subgroups are small, or treatment capacity is limited, accidental imbalance can reduce precision. Stratified randomization reduces that risk. Before assignment, divide eligible units into strata using variables strongly related to the outcome or operationally important, such as prior purchase level, model-score band, region, channel eligibility, or recent activity. Randomize treatment and control separately within each stratum. This preserves random assignment while making groups more comparable on chosen dimensions. Stratification is especially useful with heterogeneous customer groups. Imagine a campaign in which the top model-score decile has a much higher baseline conversion rate. Pure randomization usually balances that decile, but chance differences can still occur. With rare conversions, even modest imbalance among high-propensity customers can materially affect the observed rate. Stratifying by score band can stabilize the comparison. The method is not a license to create dozens of tiny cells. Too many variables or overly narrow strata can leave few observations in each cell. Use a small set of pre-treatment variables chosen before outcomes are observed. Post-treatment variables must not be used because treatment may affect them. Analysis should respect the design. If treatment fractions differ across strata, a simple unweighted overall comparison may not represent the target population. Analysts may need stratum-weighted estimates or regression adjustment. Stratification also differs from selecting a high-score population. If a company first chooses only high-score customers and then randomizes within that population, the causal estimate applies primarily to that selected population and does not automatically generalize to everyone. Eligibility, targeting, randomization, and estimation are separate decisions. A good plan records the eligible population, stratification variables, assignment ratio, reproducible procedure, treatment definition, primary outcome, analysis window, and weighting rule. Randomization protects causal identification; stratification improves balance and often precision. The goal is not cosmetic similarity but a stable and interpretable experiment without sacrificing random assignment. Analysts should document the population, observation window, assumptions, and operational definition before drawing a business conclusion. A useful review separates the observed metric, the possible mechanism, and the action that follows from the evidence. This makes the analysis easier to reproduce, challenge, and communicate to stakeholders. paragraphs.zh: 繁中完整解說：本文逐步區分觀察到的數據、可能的商業機制與可支持的結論，避免把相關性、資料邊界或模型輸出直接當成因果事實。核心實務原則是先定義母體、期間與決策目的，再選擇合適的指標、實驗設計或解釋方式，最後把證據強度與下一步行動清楚連結。
paragraphs.ja: 日本語完全訳：本文は、観測されたデータ、考えられるbusiness mechanism、証拠から支持できる結論を分けて考える。相関、データ範囲、model outputをそのまま因果事実として扱わず、対象母集団・期間・意思決定目的を先に定義する。そのうえで適切な指標、実験設計、説明方法を選び、証拠の強さと次のactionを明確につなげることが実務上の要点である。
